title: The Sharpe Pint: Reverse Factoring, Quantum Foundries, and the Spotlight Effect

opening_mood.text: Morning. Grab a coffee, or if you're reading this after the market close, get a pint in. We've got a packed slate today: Warren Buffett's successor makes his first multi-billion-dollar splash, the AI hardware trade gets a massive shot of adrenaline, and geopolitical reality crashes the oil market's short-lived peace party. Here is what you need to know to look smart in the office today.

content.text: 1. Greg Abel's First Big Splash: Berkshire Hathaway Buys Taylor Morrison for $8.5B

On Sunday, Berkshire Hathaway announced an agreement to acquire Taylor Morrison Home Corp, America's sixth-largest homebuilder, in an all-cash deal valued at $8.5 billion (including debt). The offer of $72.50 per share represents a 24% premium to Friday's close. Crucially, this is the first major multi-billion-dollar acquisition led by Greg Abel since he took over as Berkshire's CEO at the start of 2026, with Warren Buffett remaining as chairman.

Why it matters: Berkshire is doubling down on the US housing market at a time when high mortgage rates and affordability pressures have kept many investors cautious. By acquiring Taylor Morrison, which operates heavily in high-growth Sun Belt markets and has its own lucrative in-house mortgage and insurance operations, Berkshire is betting on a massive cyclical recovery and structural under-supply of US housing.

The City angle: This is a textbook case of contrarian, long-term capital allocation. While the rest of the market frets over 'higher-for-longer' rates, Berkshire is using its near-$400 billion cash hoard to buy a best-in-class operator at a reasonable valuation. It also signals a broader consolidation strategy, as Berkshire already owns Clayton Properties (the 12th largest US builder).

items: What to say at work: 'This is Greg Abel's first real test as CEO, and it's classic Berkshire. Instead of chasing expensive tech, he's buying a cash-generative, asset-heavy business in a depressed cyclical sector. It shows the transition of power is functioning exactly as planned.'

Interview talking point: If asked about M&A trends, point to this as an example of strategic consolidation in fragmented industries. Homebuilders with in-house financing (like Taylor Morrison's mortgage arm) have a massive competitive advantage right now because they can offer rate buydowns to cash-strapped buyers.

content.text: 2. Dell's AI Blowout Pushes Wall Street to Historic Winning Streak

Dell Technologies shares skyrocketed 32.8% on Friday after delivering a monster earnings report that blew past Wall Street estimates and raising its full-year outlook. The catalyst? Insatiable enterprise demand for its AI-optimised servers. The rally helped propel the S&P 500 to its seventh straight daily gain and ninth consecutive winning week—the longest such streak since 2023.

Why it matters: For months, the AI trade was almost entirely about Nvidia. Dell's blowout proves that the value is successfully migrating down the food chain to the hardware and infrastructure providers who actually package these chips into enterprise-ready data centres.

The City angle: This is a classic 'picks and shovels' play. You don't need to guess which LLM will win the software race if you're the one selling the physical servers required to run them. The massive re-rating of Dell (and peers like HPE and Supermicro) shows that asset managers are actively broadening their AI exposure away from pure-play semiconductors.

items: What to say at work: 'The Dell move shows the AI trade is maturing. We're moving from speculative chip hoarding to actual enterprise deployment. If you aren't looking at the server and cooling infrastructure players, you're missing half the margin.'

Interview talking point: Use this to discuss market breadth. A nine-week winning streak for the S&P 500 driven by a broadening AI trade suggests that despite high valuations, the fundamental earnings support is still there.

content.text: 3. The Trillion-Dollar AI IPO Pipeline Gets a Reality Check

SpaceX has reportedly dialled back its target IPO valuation to at least $1.8 trillion, down from the $2 trillion-plus figure discussed in April, as it prepares to market the largest public offering in history. Meanwhile, Anthropic's latest funding round valued the company at a staggering $965 billion, officially eclipsing rival OpenAI's prior secondary market valuation of $730 billion.

Why it matters: We are on the cusp of a historic, highly concentrated mega-IPO wave. Between SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic, public markets are being asked to absorb over $3 trillion in combined valuation. SpaceX's valuation trim suggests that even for Elon Musk's rocket giant, institutional investors are starting to push back on aggressive private-market multiples.

The City angle: For investment banks and buy-side desks, this is the ultimate test of liquidity and valuation discipline. Private venture capital has run out of room, and these companies must transition to public markets. However, public investors will demand actual path-to-profitability metrics that private VCs happily ignored.

items: What to say at work: 'SpaceX trimming its target to $1.8 trillion is a healthy sign of price discovery. Public markets aren't going to just swallow private-market fantasy numbers whole, especially with high capital costs.'

Interview talking point: If asked about the IPO market, discuss the structural challenges of these mega-listings. Explain how lockup structures and float restrictions are designed to protect early insiders, and why retail investors buying at the open need to be incredibly cautious.

content.text: 4. US-Iran Strikes Shatter Ceasefire Hopes, Jolt Oil Prices

Oil prices jumped over 3% on Monday morning, with Brent crude climbing back to $93.64. The spike followed U.S. airstrikes on Iranian military sites in retaliation for Tehran shooting down an American drone. The escalation completely shattered market optimism from last week, when traders had priced in a tentative 60-day ceasefire extension.

Why it matters: Geopolitical risk premiums are notoriously volatile, but this strike reminds markets that the Strait of Hormuz—the world's most critical energy chokepoint—remains highly fragile. The sudden reversal in oil prices also complicates the global inflation outlook.

The City angle: This is a direct headache for central banks. April's US headline PCE inflation accelerated to 3.8% YoY, largely driven by energy costs. If oil remains elevated due to persistent US-Iran friction, any hopes of the Fed or the Bank of England aggressively cutting rates in the second half of the year will quickly evaporate.

items: What to say at work: 'The market was way too quick to price in a peace dividend last week. The physical energy system and geopolitical realities don't heal as fast as paper futures contracts.'

Interview talking point: This is a prime example of macro-correlation. Explain how a geopolitical event in the Middle East directly impacts bond yields: higher oil -> higher inflation expectations -> upward pressure on the 10-year Treasury yield -> delayed central bank rate cuts.

content.text: 5. IBM's Quantum Leap: A $2B Foundry and the Rise of State Venture Capital

IBM shares surged 10% in pre-market trading on Monday, continuing a massive run that saw the stock gain nearly 30% in May. The momentum stems from the U.S. Department of Commerce proposing a $1 billion CHIPS Act award to help IBM build 'Anderon' in Albany, New York—America's first purpose-built, 300mm quantum wafer foundry. IBM is matching the grant with $1 billion of its own cash.

Why it matters: This is not a standard research grant. The U.S. government is taking minority equity stakes in these quantum companies, effectively acting as a state-backed venture capitalist. It signals that quantum computing is now officially treated as a critical national security asset rather than a futuristic lab experiment.

The City angle: IBM has quietly transitioned from a legacy enterprise tech story into a genuine quantum and AI infrastructure leader. By establishing Anderon as a 'pure-play' foundry, IBM plans to manufacture quantum chips for multiple hardware vendors globally, positioning itself as the 'TSMC of quantum.'

items: What to say at work: 'The US government taking equity stakes in quantum firms is a massive shift in industrial policy. It's no longer just about funding research; it's about the state securing commercial ownership of the next computing paradigm.'

Interview talking point: If asked about emerging tech sectors to watch, point to quantum computing. Explain that with IBM targeting fault-tolerant quantum systems by 2029, the commercialisation timeline is accelerating much faster than public markets currently appreciate.

content.text: 6. Corient Creates a $500B Wealth Management Titan

US-based wealth giant Corient completed its acquisitions of prominent UK-based multi-family offices Stonehage Fleming and Stanhope Capital Group on June 1. The combined entity now manages a staggering $508 billion in assets, making Corient the world's largest independent, non-bank wealth manager focused on ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) clients.

Why it matters: The wealth management industry is undergoing a massive, private-equity-backed consolidation wave. Boutique multi-family offices are finding it increasingly difficult to deal with rising regulatory costs and the global demands of ultra-wealthy clients on a standalone basis.

The City angle: This deal is a major land grab in the European and Middle Eastern wealth space. Corient is exporting its private partnership model globally, giving clients access to a massive, integrated platform rather than relying on a single boutique advisor. It also represents a major shift of UHNW assets away from traditional investment banks.

items: What to say at work: 'The Corient deal is proof that scale is the only thing that matters in wealth management now. The boutique multi-family office model is being swallowed by global platforms backed by massive institutional capital.'

Interview talking point: If interviewing for a wealth management or private banking role, discuss this consolidation trend. Explain how regulatory compliance costs and the need for sophisticated cross-border tax and investment services are driving independent firms to merge.

content.text: The Weekend Hangover: Oil Surges as Ceasefire Hopes Evaporate

Right, grab a coffee. If you went into the weekend thinking we were on the brink of Middle Eastern peace and a smooth path to Fed rate cuts, Monday morning has delivered a proper cold shower. On Friday, Wall Street was in absolute party mode. The S&P 500 notched its ninth consecutive winning week, closing at a record 7,580.07, while the Dow crossed the 51,000 milestone for the first time in history, finishing at 51,032.34. The catalyst? A massive 32.8% weekly surge in Dell Technologies (DELL) after an AI-fueled earnings blowout, combined with intense optimism that a 60-day US-Iran ceasefire deal was about to be signed.

But as is so often the case lately, the weekend had other ideas. The geopolitical risk premium, which had briefly evaporated on Friday, came roaring back on Monday morning. Brent crude jumped over 3% to nearly $94 a barrel, and WTI crude pushed back above $90. The immediate trigger was a sharp escalation in the Gulf: the US conducted 'self-defence' strikes against Iranian radar and drone control installations along the Strait of Hormuz after Iran downed a US MQ-1 Reaper drone. Iran retaliated by targeting a US base and launching missile strikes toward Kuwait, while Israel ordered troops deeper into southern Lebanon. Just like that, the easy-money ceasefire narrative has been put on ice.
The Cross-Asset Read: AI Gravity vs. Geopolitical Friction

Normally, a 3% spike in oil and escalating Middle East skirmishes would have equity traders hitting the sell button. Instead, US stock futures are holding remarkably firm, with S&P 500 futures up 0.3% and Nasdaq futures up 0.2% on Monday morning. Why the resilience? It is the sheer gravity of the tech trade. Jensen Huang has been out dismissing AI disruption fears, Nvidia is reportedly eyeing the PC market, and Microsoft is up in premarket. Equities are essentially saying: 'We will pay more for fuel if we must, as long as the data centres keep humming.' But underneath the surface, there is a massive bifurcation. While the Dow and S&P 500 hit records on Friday, the small-cap Russell 2000 actually fell 0.59% to 2,919.34. This is a classic two-speed market: mega-cap tech is insulated by massive cash piles and secular AI demand, while smaller companies are getting squeezed by the 'higher-for-longer' reality.
Macro Reality Check: Rate Cuts Are Off the Table

The macro backdrop isn't offering any relief either. The April PCE inflation data released late last week showed headline PCE at 3.8% and core PCE ticking up to 3.3% YoY. That is nearly double the Fed's 2% target. With the 10-year Treasury yield creeping back up to 4.46% on Monday morning, any hopes of a Fed rate cut this summer are officially dead. If you're in an interview or a client meeting today, the talking point is clear: we are in a structural 'resilient but squeezed' economy where AI capex is keeping the headline indices afloat, but the average corporate borrower is feeling the vice tighten.

content.text: The Trojan Horse of Working Capital: Reverse Factoring

Imagine you owe your local pub £100 for a hefty Thursday night tab. Instead of paying them, you get your rich mate, Barclays, to pay the pub £95 right now, and you promise to pay Barclays £100 in three months' time. You walk away telling everyone your 'accounts payable' are in great shape and you've got plenty of cash in hand. In the corporate world, this is called reverse factoring (or supply chain finance). It is the financial equivalent of wearing a fake Rolex: it looks great from a distance, but if you look closely, something is seriously off.

Historically, this was a niche treasury tool. But over the last decade, it has become the go-to method for companies to window-dress their balance sheets, artificially boost their operating cash flows, and hide what is effectively bank debt in the operating liabilities section.
How the Magic Trick Works
In a standard supply chain finance arrangement, three things happen:

items: The Buyer (our company) buys goods from a Supplier.
The Bank steps in and pays the Supplier early, usually at a small discount (e.g., £98 instead of £100). The Supplier is happy because they get paid instantly.
The Buyer pays the Bank back later—often stretching their payment terms from a standard 30 days to 90 or 120 days.

content.text: Here is the catch: because this transaction involves paying a supplier, accounting standards historically allowed companies to keep this liability classified as 'Trade Payables' rather than 'Short-Term Debt'. When the company finally pays the bank, it is classified as an operating cash outflow, not a financing cash outflow.

This creates two massive distortions. First, Net Debt looks artificially low because trade payables aren't included in typical leverage calculations (like Net Debt/EBITDA). Second, when a company first sets up or aggressively expands one of these programmes, its trade payables spike. In the cash flow statement, an increase in payables is a cash inflow. Voila: operating cash flow is magically inflated, making the business look like a cash-generating machine when it's actually just borrowing from the future.
Why This Matters in Asset Management and Credit

If you are analysing a company, ignoring this is a fast track to getting burned. When a company's operations deteriorate, banks don't just stand there. If they get nervous, they will quietly pull the reverse factoring facility. Suddenly, the company has to pay its suppliers on normal, short terms. The working capital benefit reverses instantly, creating a massive cash drain. This is exactly what triggered the spectacular collapses of UK construction giant Carillion in 2018 and Spanish clean-energy firm Abengoa. It wasn't a slow decline; it was a sudden liquidity cliff.

Thankfully, the regulators have caught on. Under both IFRS (via IASB amendments to IAS 7 and IFRS 7) and US GAAP (via FASB ASU 2022-04), companies are now required to disclose the key terms of these 'supplier finance arrangements' and where they are presented on the balance sheet. But they still don't always force them into the 'Debt' line. You have to go hunting in the footnotes.
The Interview Question & How to Sound Like a Pro

If you are interviewing for a buy-side equity role, private equity, or private credit, this is a goldmine topic. An interviewer might ask: 'How would you assess whether a company's working capital improvements are sustainable?'
Don't just talk about inventory management or squeezing suppliers. Bring this up:

I’d look closely at the cash conversion cycle, specifically Days Payable Outstanding (DPO). If DPO has shot up significantly while peers are flat, I'd immediately dig into the footnotes for supplier finance or reverse factoring arrangements. If they are using these facilities, I would adjust the balance sheet by reclassifying those payables as debt, and adjust the cash flow statement to treat the changes as financing cash flows. Otherwise, you're understating leverage and overstating organic cash generation.
The Pub Conversation Starter

Next time someone pitches you a 'high-quality compounder' with an incredibly long payable cycle and pristine leverage, ask them: 'Is that operational efficiency, or is it just bank debt in a trench coat?'

content.text: The "Cheat Code" for Portfolio Optimisation: Decision by Supervised Learning (DSL)

If you have ever spent a Friday afternoon watching a quadratic optimiser throw a tantrum because two tech stocks decided to correlate at 0.99, you will know the pain of traditional portfolio construction. Historically, quants have had two choices. First, Prediction-Focused Learning (PFL): train a model to predict asset returns, then feed those predictions into a mean-variance optimiser. The problem? Small errors in return predictions lead to wild, unstable swings in portfolio weights. Second, Decision-Focused Learning (DFL): train a neural network where the loss function is the actual portfolio performance (like the Sharpe ratio). This requires backpropagating through the optimisation step itself. It is mathematically elegant, but computationally, it is like trying to push a grand piano up the stairs of Covent Garden tube station—slow, painful, and prone to crashing.

Enter "Decision by Supervised Learning" (DSL), a remarkably clever workaround presented at the CIKM FinAI Workshop. Instead of predicting returns or backpropagating through a finicky optimiser, DSL reframes portfolio construction as a straightforward supervised classification problem. Since a long-only portfolio's weights are non-negative and sum to one, they behave exactly like a probability distribution. DSL exploits this by precomputing the "perfect" target portfolio weights (e.g., the maximum Sharpe or Sortino portfolio) historically on training data. It then trains a neural network to map current market features directly to those target weights using standard cross-entropy loss. To stop the model from overfitting to historical noise, it uses a Deep Ensemble—training multiple networks with different random seeds and averaging their outputs to slash variance.
How It Works in the Real World

Imagine you are running a multi-asset tactical allocation fund. Instead of trying to predict next month's exact returns for equities, bonds, gold, and commodities, you look back at historical windows and calculate what the optimal asset weights should have been. You then train your model to look at macro indicators (inflation, yield curve slope, credit spreads) and directly output those optimal weights. Because cross-entropy is a convex loss function, training is lightning-fast and incredibly stable compared to traditional reinforcement learning or differentiable optimisation.
Mini Technical Example
The Paper Angle

This approach comes from a paper titled "Decision by Supervised Learning with Deep Ensembles: A Practical Framework for Robust Portfolio Optimization" by Juhyeong Kim et al.. The authors backtested the model across various market universes and found it consistently outperformed both traditional mean-variance baselines and complex end-to-end machine learning models. Crucially, they showed that as you increase the size of the Deep Ensemble, the out-of-sample portfolio variance drops significantly, leading to much smoother, more investable allocations. The code is fully open-source on GitHub under the repository DSLwDE/DSLwDE.
The Pub / Interview Conversation Starter

Next time someone at work starts hyping up complex reinforcement learning or differentiable optimisers for asset allocation, hit them with this: "Why are we wasting compute backpropagating through a non-convex optimiser when we can just precompute the optimal historical targets and train a deep ensemble using cross-entropy? It treats portfolio weights as a probability distribution, trains in seconds, and the ensemble averaging naturally dampens the out-of-sample turnover." It shows you understand both the practical engineering bottlenecks of ML and the mathematical structure of portfolio constraints.
The Catch

The obvious limitation is that this setup is naturally built for long-only portfolios because of the softmax/probability assumption. If you want to run a long-short market-neutral book, standard cross-entropy won't work out of the box because you have negative weights. You would have to pivot to a different loss function like Mean Squared Error, which loses some of the elegant probabilistic properties. Additionally, if your historical target portfolios are calculated poorly (e.g., if you don't account for transaction costs when calculating the "perfect" historical weights), your model will happily learn to replicate a highly active, expensive, and ultimately unprofitable strategy.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: Right, let's talk about the elephant in the room: AI trading. Every week, some preprint drops on arXiv claiming a GPT-powered agent has generated a 4.0 Sharpe ratio by reading earnings transcripts. It sounds amazing. It makes you feel like you're living in the stone age with your multi-factor linear models. But before you bin your career and hand your capital to a chatbot, you need to read this paper.
The Paper

Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration (arXiv:2602.14233, Feb 2026) by Yaxuan Kong, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Stefan Zohren, and a heavyweight team from Oxford, Man Group, and the University of Florida.
Why This One?

Because it is a massive, beautifully researched reality check. The authors are not AI luddites—Lopez-Lira wrote the seminal paper on ChatGPT stock predictability, and Zohren is a leading quant at Oxford and Man Group. They know their stuff. But they have had enough of the shoddy backtesting hygiene in AI-for-finance research. They reviewed 164 papers published between 2023 and 2025 and found that almost all of them are accidentally cheating. The paper systematically dismantles these breakthroughs by exposing five classic financial biases that LLMs are uniquely prone to.
The Five Cheats (and How LLMs Pull Them Off)

items: 1. Look-Ahead Bias (The Time Traveller): LLMs are trained on massive historical datasets. If you backtest a model on 2023 data, but the model's training cutoff was 2025, it already knows which companies survived, who won the elections, and that Nvidia went to the moon. This is parametric look-ahead. Even if you prompt it carefully, the future is baked into its weights.

2. Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Town): Many papers evaluate their LLM trading strategies using the current constituents of the S&P 500 or FTSE 100. They completely ignore the companies that went bust, merged, or got delisted during the backtest period. It turns out, avoiding bankrupt companies makes any strategy look like a work of genius.

3. Narrative Bias (The Monday Morning Quarterback): LLMs are literally designed to tell coherent stories. If you ask a model to analyse a past event, it will construct a beautifully logical, highly convincing narrative explaining why a stock moved, using hindsight. In reality, the point-in-time data available at that exact millisecond was a noisy, confusing mess.

4. Objective Bias (The Confident Bullshitter): Standard LLMs are aligned using RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) to be helpful and confident. In finance, the correct answer is often 'I don't know, the signal-to-noise ratio is too low.' But the model's training forces it to take a guess and sound incredibly convincing while doing so, leading to highly confident, disastrous trades.

5. Cost Bias (The Slippage Mirage): Almost all academic papers report gross returns, assuming zero transaction costs, zero bid-ask spread slippage, and zero borrow costs. If your LLM strategy has 500% annual turnover, a tiny 5 bps execution cost will turn your beautiful upward-sloping equity curve into a straight line to bankruptcy.

content.text: The Damning Stats
The authors' review of those 164 papers revealed some hilarious (and terrifying) gaps in basic financial hygiene:

items: Only 26.8% of the papers even acknowledged look-ahead bias.
A microscopic 1.2% of studies accounted for survivorship bias.
Practically none of them factored in realistic transaction costs or execution slippage.

content.text: These biases break financial tasks in distinct ways and they often compound to create an illusion of validity... If any requirement fails, the reported result can only support a stress test interpretation or a proof of concept, and it cannot support a claim of deployable alpha.
What to Skim

If you are not a machine learning engineer, you can safely skim the heavy mathematical formulations of the biases and the training loss functions. Instead, head straight for Section 3 (where they define the five biases in detail) and the Structural Validity Checklist in the appendix. It is the ultimate checklist for calling BS on any AI vendor.
How to Use This at Work

If you are a quant, portfolio manager, or developer, you are going to be pitched agentic AI trading systems by vendors, or asked by your boss to spin up an LLM sentiment model. Use this paper as your shield. The authors have kindly provided a Structural Validity Checklist. It is a binary filter: if a system fails even one check, it is a toy, not a trading strategy.
What to Say Over a Pint

We need to stop treating LLM backtests like traditional quantitative backtests. If the model has already read the history books, its alpha isn't predictive skill—it's just a very expensive, GPU-burning memory recall. Before we allocate a single pound to an AI agent, we need to run a parametric look-ahead audit.
The Sharpe Pint Take

This is the most important paper on financial AI of the year. It does not say LLMs are useless; it says our methods for testing them are broken. It is incredibly easy to look like Jim Simons when you are a time traveller. If you want to build something that actually survives in production, you have to stop grading your models on open-book exams.

content.text: It’s 11:00 PM on a Thursday. You’re staring at slide 43 of a pitch deck, sweat on your brow, trying to decide if a client logo is two pixels too far to the left. You are absolutely convinced that if the Managing Director or the client notices this, your career in the City is finished, you’ll be exiled to a back-office role in Leeds, and you'll never buy a pint in London again.

Welcome to the Spotlight Effect. It’s one of the most common psychological taxes on your mental health in high-pressure environments, and learning to switch it off is the ultimate corporate sanity-saver.
The Barry Manilow Experiment

The term was coined in 2000 by psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec, and Kenneth Savitsky. In a famous experiment, they forced college students to wear a highly embarrassing T-shirt—featuring the face of Barry Manilow—and walk into a room full of peers. The T-shirt wearers were convinced that at least 50% of the room would notice their cringe-worthy attire. In reality? Only 23% did.

This happens because of egocentric bias. Because we spend 100% of our lives inside our own heads, we are the main character in our own movie. We naturally assume we’re at least a prominent supporting actor in everyone else’s. But here is the liberating, beautiful truth: everyone else is also the main character in their own movie. They aren’t looking at your metaphorical Barry Manilow T-shirt; they are too busy panicking about whether their own voice cracked when they said 'synergies' in the morning stand-up.
How to Use This in the City

items: The 'Don't Point Out the Stain' Rule: If you make a minor, non-critical mistake—like a formatting glitch on a slide or a tiny typo in a pitch deck appendix—do not send a frantic follow-up email pointing it out. By doing so, you are literally dragging their spotlight to the error. If you stay quiet, there is a 90% chance they will slide right past it.

Ask the 'Stupid' Question: The fear of looking foolish keeps many smart junior-to-mid-level professionals silent in meetings. If you ask a question that turns out to be slightly basic, nobody is going to remember it. They are too busy thinking about what they want to order from Deliveroo or how to phrase their own next point.

Take More Calculated Risks: Pitching a non-consensus trade or a quirky investment thesis can feel terrifying because you assume everyone will remember if it goes wrong. In reality, the market moves incredibly fast. Yesterday’s bad pitch is tomorrow’s fish-and-chip paper. People have remarkably short memories for other people's failures.

content.text: One Line to Remember
Nobody is looking at your misaligned logo on slide 43; they are too busy worrying about their own slides.
